contract: THE WIRE SHAPE OF A MOUNT-INDEPENDENT ATTENTION VERDICT, frozen here so the Rust producer and
the TypeScript consumer fail TOGETHER rather than silently agreeing to disagree.
WHY A SHARED FIXTURE AT ALL. AGENTS.md records the measured failure this exists to prevent: two
agents built the two halves of a Rust->TS payload in parallel against a frozen field list, both
suites passed, the merge was clean, and the shipped feature never once ran. An all-or-nothing
parser that rejects one field discards the WHOLE payload and falls back to its 'we did not look'
default -- with nothing logged. So: src-tauri asserts its serializer PRODUCES these bytes, and
the TS parser asserts it ACCEPTS these bytes. One file, two suites, no drift.
NO OPTIONAL FIELDS, DELIBERATELY. A Rust `Option::None` crosses the wire as `null`, never as an
absent key, and TypeScript's `field?: T` means `T | undefined` -- which does not include null.
Every field here is unconditionally present so that trap has nowhere to live. Keep it that way:
a new field owes a value in every sample below, not an `Option`.
THE THREE VERDICTS, and the boundary between them is the whole point:
awaiting   -- a human is owed an answer. The rendered grid carries a prompt the classifier
recognises (nudge_gate::screen_awaits_input).
unreadable -- WE COULD NOT TELL. A full-screen app owns the buffer and it is not Claude Code's
own prompt, so no claim about this agent can be made. This is NOT 'calm'.
Reporting an unreadable screen as calm is the founder's bug: an agent that needs
him renders as fine because nothing could see it.
calm       -- the grid was read and carries no prompt. A POSITIVE reading, not an absence.
delegating -- the grid was read, carries no prompt, AND shows live delegated work: Claude
Code's own `N background task(s) live` footer or its running-subagent roster.
The founder's rule is that DELEGATED WORK COUNTS AS ACTIVITY, so a row holding
this must not be gray. It is produced ONLY where `calm` would otherwise be, so
it can never mask an `awaiting`; a consumer may treat it as `calm` and be
merely less useful, never wrong.
gone       -- THIS AGENT'S TERMINAL NO LONGER EXISTS. Not a statement about a screen; there
is no screen. Discard any reading held for this agent. It exists because the
producer emits on CHANGE, and 'the agent stopped existing' is a change the
other three cannot carry -- without it a spun-down agent whose last reading
was `awaiting` stays RAISED forever against a terminal that is gone, with
nothing on the wire able to retract it. `alternate` is always false here.
`alternate` travels alongside the verdict rather than being folded into it, because 'Claude Code
is on the alternate buffer showing its own picker' is `awaiting` WITH `alternate: true` -- the
consumer must not have to re-derive that from the verdict alone.
`atMs` IS THE ONSET OF THE CURRENT VERDICT -- when it STARTED holding, not when it was last
observed. NO NEWS MEANS IT STILL HOLDS. This is the only meaning both channels can express: the
producer emits on CHANGE, so an unchanged reading sends nothing and the event stream can carry
nothing but onset. Making the stored row as-of was tried and reverted, because it left `list()`
(the startup seed) disagreeing with the stream for the same agent, with nothing on the wire to
tell the two meanings apart. Samples below carry DIFFERENT values so a consumer that ignores
the field cannot be told apart from one that honours it.
SO DO NOT KEY A STALENESS RULE ON `atMs`. An old stamp means the verdict has held for a long
time, which for `awaiting` is the row that most needs attention, not the least. Reading it as
decay discards precisely the agent who has been waiting longest.
NO VERDICT EXPIRES ON THE CONSUMER'S CLOCK, and that is a decision rather than an omission. The
producer ticks once a second per live session and retracts with `gone`, so a reading that stops
arriving means the app is down -- in which case every row is stale and a per-row rule buys
nothing. A consumer-side expiry would ALSO re-create the bug this channel exists to fix: it
would silently drop the `awaiting` of an agent that has been waiting longest.
THERE IS NO `no-viewport` VERDICT, deliberately. `nudge_gate::write_refusal` has that arm for a
screen it was handed as `None`; this producer never asks about an agent it has no observer for,
because the observer registry IS the population. No PTY means no event -- not an event saying
there is no PTY. The `gone` retraction is what covers a PTY that goes away after being observed.
AN UNPARSEABLE OR UNKNOWN-VERDICT PAYLOAD MUST NEVER RESOLVE TO `calm`. A newer producer can
always emit a token an older consumer does not know, and reading that as 'fine' reproduces the
founder's bug through the parser instead of through the mount. The consumer drops the payload
for that ONE agent (leaving whatever it already held), warns once, and never lets one bad
payload discard the others -- which is the all-or-nothing failure named above. Dropping is safe
here precisely BECAUSE `unreadable` is itself inert: there is no state an unknown token could
have reached that says more than 'no opinion'.

samples.why: An ordinary Claude Code question menu on the normal buffer. The classic red case.
Claude Code's own picker on the ALTERNATE buffer -- readable, so a real claim is made.
A full-screen app we cannot parse. The founder's 'unknown-and-therefore-needs-attention'.
UNREADABLE ON THE NORMAL BUFFER -- the PTY reader is parked by flow control, so the grid is arbitrarily stale. Present so a consumer cannot key its unreadable handling on `alternate`.
Read the grid, found no prompt. The ONLY verdict that may lower a row.

DELEGATED WORK IS VISIBLE -- subagents are running, so this agent is ACTIVE even though its own turn produced nothing. `apps/desktop/shared/delegated-work.fixture.json` holds the screens; this pins the WIRE TOKEN both halves must agree on.
The agent's PTY was swept. The retraction, so a held verdict cannot outlive its terminal.
